Rodas4 on the pendulum shows an order between 4.5 and 4.9 over every halving clean of rounding, not 4: its leading fourth-order error term is very small on this problem, so the fifth-order term rules the errors that can be measured. notes: infer fits one-row-lagged, additive models (with optional powers of a source and a source-target product) by ridge regression, after a skeleton of lag-1 partial correlations with a fixed threshold of 0.1 (docs/causalInference.md). Datasets inside that model class are recovered well; the ones outside it are included to show where it fails, and say why in their rows.

False edges in the recoverable datasets are reverse edges with small rates (the shrinkage effect docs/causalInference.md describes): each row gives the largest false edge's rate beside the smallest true rate. Less noise does not always help: the diamond with the least downstream noise (σ = 0.5) has two (x2 → x1, x3 → x1), because x2 and x3 then follow x1 closely enough to predict it, and it scores below the same diamond at σ = 2. A hidden common cause is the exception: its false edges are as strong as true ones, and nothing in the data can tell them apart.

A variable with no cause found gets no equation at all, by design (docs/causalInference.md, 'Replaying recorded values for input columns'); the own-rate error is measured only over variables with a true cause.

Rates are compared in the engine's own units, per second of the CSV's time column: an edge's terms, and a variable's own rate (its self-lag coefficient less one, over Δt). For the continuous-time datasets the true rates are the system matrix A; infer reports (Φ - I)/Δt for the sampled transition Φ = exp(A Δt), which equals A only as A Δt → 0, while at fine sampling the skeleton finds nothing: there is no sampling interval at which both the structure and the rates are right.

notes: The reference's own error: the 70-digit Taylor solution agrees with its lower-order, 50-digit check to 6.0e-30 over 40 s; SciPy's DOP853 at rtol = atol = 1e-12 departs from it by 1 % of the range at 33.64 s, so a double-precision reference at that tolerance would itself be useless beyond then.

The attractor's statistics from the reference ensemble (200 runs of 500 s): mean of z 23.5501, standard deviation of z 8.6222, root mean square of x 7.9246, largest Lyapunov exponent 0.9059 /s (Viswanath: 0.9056). One 500 s run scatters about them by 0.038, 0.038, 0.007 and 0.007 /s, so a score within about 2 σ is as close as one run can be expected to come.

Three nodes, one per variable, cannot be written: a relationship reads only its two ends, and the equations of y and z each read both other variables. The split model is x as one node and y, z as another.

referenceProvenance.method: Taylor series in multiple precision (mpmath): order 40, step 1/256 s, 70 digits; checked against order 30, step 1/128 s, 50 digits. Statistics: an ensemble solved by solve_ivp DOP853 at rtol = atol = 1e-10; the Lyapunov exponent by Benettin's method.
referenceProvenance.literature: Viswanath, D. (1998). Global errors of numerical ODE solvers and Lyapunov's theory of stability (PhD thesis, Cornell): 0.905630 to six figures.
